headline: Water questions, answered in three sentences
lead: For teams running or planning Purified Water (PW) systems: one question per note, answered first, clause named. Latest: polypropylene or stainless steel for a PW loop.

items.d: Our standard says stainless steel. Can a polypropylene loop carry our Purified Water?

items.t: After a water observation: what inspectors ask for

blocks.h: Polypropylene or stainless steel for a PW loop
blocks.intro: Polypropylene suits an ambient PW loop, sanitized chemically. Water for Injection (WFI) or a stainless standard needs stainless. Limits, sampling and release are unchanged.
rows: The loop carries Purified Water (PW) for non-sterile products, rinses and washing.
The loop carries Water for Injection (WFI), or feeds a pure steam generator.
It names outcomes: materials compatible with PW and the sanitizing agent, and drainable.
It names 316L stainless steel for product contact, and a deviation is not an option.
Your auditors accept a plastic loop backed by its maker's ratings and your sanitization records.
A client's quality agreement names stainless steel for water contact.
The cause is known and designed out: joints or supports for expansion.
No cause was found, and your engineers will not accept plastic again.

items.q: How is each note written and reviewed?
items.a: A named engineer writes each note from a real question; a named reviewer checks it before publication. Each claim names standard, clause and edition.

items.q: Can we cite a note in our validation documents?
items.a: No: cite the standard, not the note. A note is our reading of the clause; your quality unit decides how it applies to your site.

items.q: What happens when a standard changes?
items.a: We review and update the note and its review date. If the answer changes, the note says what and when. Errors get a dated correction line.

blocks.h: Get each technical note by email
blocks.intro: Occasional emails; confirmed by email first; no sales mail; your address never shared.
